opening.headline: When deciding where to execute a continuously running agent, compare whether the managed runtime or direct hosting is responsible.
body: Agents need a stable execution environment if they are to read files and execute commands for several hours. While directly setting up the environment provides greater control, it also requires me to manage servers, security, and scalability. Using a managed environment reduces operational burden but limits control to the scope defined by the product.

In this course, after learning about the components provided by managed agents and the concept of sandboxes, we compare Managed Agents, Agent Runtime, and direct self-hosting of the Agent SDK in a single table. We then examine how responsibilities differ when operating within a self-hosted sandbox and explore their application in overnight job scenarios.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the responsibility allocation between managed runtime and direct hosting.
Can assess runtimes that match operational burden and control levels

screens.title: Where should the agent that runs all night be executed?
screens.lead: First, let's examine the choices encountered when deploying an agent into the operational environment. Read the following scenario and consider what criteria would be necessary.

visual.alt: A horizontal balance diagram spanning from the low operational burden and low control management model to the high operational burden and high control direct hosting model.
labels: Managed environment: low operational burden / defined control scope of the product
Direct hosting: High operational burden / Wide control scope

paragraphs: Let's consider an agent that reads files from the storage for several hours, executes commands, aggregates results, and generates a report in the morning. Such an agent needs a secure workspace to safely execute commands and a continuous environment that can run uninterrupted between intermediate steps.

Setting up the execution environment directly increases control. Instead, I have to manage the server, security, and scalability. Conversely, using a managed environment reduces operational burden. Instead, the scope of control is limited to what the product provides.
Ultimately, runtime must be determined between operational burden and control level. The question this course addresses is this: how can we compare the options based on who is responsible for what?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Determining where to execute an agent—is this a server selection problem or a responsibility delegation problem? We'll revisit this answer at the end of the class.

screens.outro: First, let me recall where my agent is currently located.

screens.title: Where is the agent currently being executed?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Where is my agent currently running? What happens to the task if the execution environment is terminated or restarted?
items.answer: During development, it's sufficient to run it on my computer. However, when dealing with long-running tasks similar to overnight work, it's important to verify whether the work continues after the environment is restarted. If it does not continue, we must first determine who is responsible.

items.prompt: Where are the files created by the agent and the work logs stored?
items.answer: If file systems and conversation logs exist only on the disk of the execution environment, they are deleted along with the environment when it is removed. Managed services may store such states on the service side, but self-hosted solutions must directly design their own retention mechanisms.

items.prompt: Is there a designated location where data must reside due to security or regulatory requirements?
items.answer: If data cannot leave the internal network or access to internal services is required, the options become limited. Such requirements serve as the most clear-cut criterion for determining control levels, and this course will address this scenario separately.

screens.outro: Now that I've organized my thoughts, I'll examine the components that constitute a managed agent.

screens.title: Managed agents and sandbox environment
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the terms highlighted below, a brief description will appear. Please review each term one by one.

visual.alt: Agent definition executed within an Environment session, illustrating the configuration for exchanging apps and events with the environment.
labels: Agent (model, system prompt, tool, MCP server, skill)
Events (user messages, tool results, status notifications)

data.text: Claude Managed Agents is a service that manages agent loops and tool execution, as well as the execution environment. It consists of four conceptual components. Agent defines the model, system prompt, tools, MCP server, and skills, and is created once with an ID to be referenced across multiple sessions. Environment specifies where the session runs—either Anthropic's managed cloud sandbox or self-hosted infrastructure on the user's own infrastructure sandbox. Session is an agent instance that performs specific tasks within the environment. Events represents the messages exchanged between the application and the agent. sandbox is an isolated workspace in which the agent executes commands and handles files. Sessions can run for extended periods and persist across interruptions, with conversation history, sandbox state, and outputs stored on the server.

terms.tip: Model, system prompt, tools, MCP server, and skill definitions. Create them once and retrieve them by ID across multiple sessions.
This configures where the session will run: either a cloud sandbox managed by Anthropic or a self-hosted sandbox directly operated by the organization.
An executing agent instance that performs a specific task within an environment and produces output.
Messages exchanged between the application and the agent. This includes user input, tool results, and status notifications.
An isolated workspace where an agent executes commands and handles files. A container is a typical example.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the concept, let's compare the three hosting methods side by side in a single table.

screens.title: Compare three hosting methods in the same table
screens.lead: The following table compares three methods under the same item. Read it horizontally to verify how each method differs for the same item.

data.caption: Comparison of Responsibility Allocation in Agent Hosting Models
rows: Agent Loop and Execution Infrastructure
Anthropic operates the agent loop and sandbox.
A fully managed runtime handles agent deployment, operation, and scaling.
The SDK launches a sub-process of the Claude CLI, and I operate the container.
How to upload
Define the agent and environment and start a session.
Can be deployed as a container image or Dockerfile, and any language and framework can be used as long as it can be containerized.
Deploys applications and SDKs directly into a container.
Process Model
The session runs within the environment.
Sends an API request to the deployed agent
An agent is a long-lived process that corresponds to one subordinate process and maintains local state.
State preservation
Conversation logs, sandbox status, and outputs are stored on the server.
Functions are provided to manage and delete deployed agents.
Session logs, memory files, and working directory are stored on the container disk and are lost upon restart.
What I am designing
Agent definition, tools, network rules
Container and access control (IAM, VPC-SC) configuration
Resource allocation, session persistence, tenant-level expansion entirely
Applicable cases
When long execution time and minimal operational overhead are required
When you want to deploy it as a managed service in the cloud environment
When controlling all parts including the agent loop
data.notes: The largest difference in the table is the second-to-last row. The more to the right you go, the more work I have to design. To directly host and maintain state, session records must be handled via a SessionStore adapter, while memory files and work directories must be addressed using separate strategies such as mounted volumes or object storage synchronization.

screens.outro: Next, we will examine the point where responsibilities divide within the same managed service.

screens.title: Responsibility Sharing: Cloud Environment and On-Premises Sandbox
screens.lead: Compare the responsibilities that vary depending on who operates the sandbox, by examining the transition between two states.

visual.alt: Two configurations showing different placement of model, service, and tool execution locations in cloud environments and on-premises sandboxes.
labels: My infrastructure: worker + sandbox (bash, file utilities)

states.label: cloud environment
states.body: The tools and code run within **Anthropic's sandbox**. I do not manage anything. Mounting of files and GitHub repositories, mounting of memory stores, and the lifecycle of the sandbox are all managed by Anthropic, while network rules are set at the environment level. This is the default option when there's no need for the tools to run on my infrastructure. While it incurs the lowest operational overhead, the tools must operate within the scope provided by the sandbox.

states.label: Self-hosted sandbox
states.body: Claude is handled by Anthropic, while the worker runs bash and file tools on my infrastructure and returns the results. In return, I manage the worker host, including security hardening, network restrictions, and environment keys used for authentication. Files and processes remain on my worker, but tool results are delivered via a service so that the model can access them. Conversation records are also stored in the service, meaning not all data remains internal. Consider this approach if access to an internal network service is required, if files cannot leave the network, or if execution must occur under organizational audit controls. Some features, such as pre-installed cloud runtime environments and file resources, are not available.

screens.outro: Since the comparison criteria are established, let's apply them to the overnight work case.

screens.title: Explanation: Deriving environmental conditions required for overnight work sessions
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: A hypothetical refactoring agent reads the code repository and runs tests overnight, producing a summary of changes by morning. Since no human is monitoring it, the environment must be self-stabilizing.

steps.title: Step 1: Requirement Extraction
steps.body: We summarize the requirements: it must run for several hours, require files and packages, and continue execution even after restarts. These three conditions imply that the environment must have a persistent filesystem and state preservation.

steps.title: Step 2: Option Comparison
steps.body: Managed cloud environments provide isolated containers, persistent filesystems, and conversation history storage. If the same requirements are fulfilled directly through self-hosting, you must directly design session persistence and resource allocation, as well as develop your own storage strategy to address restart scenarios.

steps.title: Step 3: Verify Control Requirements
steps.body: Now we address the control requirements. If the repository is located only within the corporate network or data cannot leave the network, consider a self-hosted sandbox running the tool within your infrastructure. In this scenario, the fact that tool results are delivered as a service remains unchanged.

steps.title: Step 4: Conclusion
steps.body: If control requirements do not exist, begin in the cloud environment. If control requirements exist, operate only the necessary components directly and delegate the rest to managed services. This approach—first identifying the required controls and then bearing only the corresponding operational burden—is a reasonable selection sequence.

screens.outro: Next, we will specifically examine what responsibilities come with choosing direct hosting.

screens.title: Explanation: Hosting directly can lead to unforeseen issues.
screens.lead: Expand each item and check one by one the tasks you need to design when directly hosting the Agent SDK.

items.title: Process Count
items.body: One agent session corresponds to one subordinate process. When N sessions are executed simultaneously, N processes are spawned, each possessing its own process tree and log file. Therefore, the container must be configured to hold the maximum number of concurrent sessions within a memory size that can be accommodated.

items.title: Separate working directory
items.body: By default, all sessions inherit the application's working directory. If the filesystem needs to be isolated between sessions, a different cwd must be specified for each session.

items.title: Session Record Retention
items.body: Session records generally do not survive restarts or movement to other nodes when stored on container disks. To maintain records across hosts, the SessionStore adapter must be configured. This storage is essential for long-running, continuously operating workloads.

items.title: Memory file and output
items.body: Output from memory files such as Claude.md and work directory artifacts is not preserved by SessionStore. Separate strategies such as mounting volumes or object storage synchronization are required.

items.title: Create control list first
items.body: The more operational burden there is, the greater the control requirements become. Therefore, before opting for direct hosting, clearly define in a list what specific controls are truly necessary. If the list is short, a managed solution may be sufficient.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the contents so far.

screens.title: The more control is required, the greater the operational burden becomes.
screens.lead: Let's revisit the initial question by reflecting on the flow of the lesson.

paragraphs: Managed runtime takes over operations and retains control over direct hosting. Responsibilities are divided into agent loop, tool execution location, state retention, and operational ownership, making the choice clear when compared.

Whether to execute an agent depends less on selecting a server and more on dividing responsibilities. Take direct ownership of only the necessary controls, and delegate the rest to the managed environment. This choice directly determines the size of operational overhead.

glossary.def: This is a model where agents and execution infrastructure are operated by the service provider.
This is a manner in which agents, their processes, and execution environments are operated by users within their own infrastructure.
An agent operates in an isolated workspace performing commands and file operations.
A process that executes tool calls within a user-hosted sandbox and returns the results from a self-hosted sandbox.
This distinguishes who is responsible for execution, security, state retention, and extension.

misconceptions.myth: In a managed environment, I have absolutely no tasks to perform.
misconceptions.fact: Agent definitions, tools, and network rules still need to be designed. The only missing component is the operational infrastructure.

misconceptions.myth: Using a self-hosted sandbox ensures that data does not leave the system.
misconceptions.fact: Files and processes remain on the worker, but tool results and conversation logs are forwarded to the service so that the model can receive them.

misconceptions.myth: Agent hosting is similar to running a general API server.
misconceptions.fact: An agent is a long-lived process with local state. The design for restart and scaling differs.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content covered in this course.
points: Managed runtime reduces operational burden and enhances control when hosting directly.
Responsibility allocation is compared based on agent loops, tool execution location, state storage, and operational principal.
Long-running tasks, isolated workspaces, and a state that can be resumed are necessary for overnight operations.
The more control is required, the greater the operational burden becomes.
closing.reflectionLead: Finally, here's a question for you to think about on your own. Please feel free to recall it at your convenience—no submission or grading is required.
closing.reflection: In my agent, what must I necessarily control, and consequently what operational burdens must I accept?

checks.q: The Agent SDK was directly hosted within the container, but the container restarted. What happens then if no separate setup is performed?
options: Session history stored on Anthropic servers is automatically restored.
Session logs remain, but the working directory is deleted.
Session logs, memory files, and working directories are deleted along with the container disk.
The agent process is automatically restored to its state prior to restart.
checks.explain: In direct hosting, each agent is a local-state-bearing process, and session logs, memory files, and work directories reside on the container disk and are lost upon restart. Persistence is designed by the user.

wrong.0: History retention on the server side is a characteristic of managed environments and is not automatic in directly hosted environments.
wrong.1: Since the record is stored on the same disk, it is also deleted together.
wrong.3: The process state does not recover automatically and a persistence strategy is required.
